## How to Use This Blind Recognition Checkpoint {#sec-cp02-how-to-use}

In Part II ([Chapter 05](../chapters/ch05-lyndon-factorization-duval-necklaces.qmd) through [Chapter 08](../chapters/ch08-runs-theorem-squares-sweep.qmd)), you built four tightly linked engines connecting lexicographical order to periodic structure:

1. **[Chapter 05 — Chen–Fox–Lyndon Factorization, Duval's Automaton, All-Prefix State Sharing & Necklace Bijections](../chapters/ch05-lyndon-factorization-duval-necklaces.qmd)**: Decomposing any string uniquely into $S = w_1 w_2 \cdots w_k$ ($w_i \in \mathcal{L}, w_1 \ge \cdots \ge w_k$) in $< 2N$ comparisons via Duval's $(i, j, k)$ pointers, extracting all-prefix CFL statistics in $O(1)$ per step via remainder state sharing $r \to r - dp$, factoring Run-Length Encoded strings in $O(M)$ time, and generating necklaces/De Bruijn cycles via Witt's formula and FKM.
2. **[Chapter 06 — The Significant Suffixes (`显著后缀`) Theorem, 1-Survivor Segment Tree Merging & Dyadic SA-RMQ](../chapters/ch06-significant-suffixes-substrings.qmd)**: Proving by tandem annihilation ($u = wu', v = w^2 u' \implies \min(u'T, vT) < uT < \max(u'T, vT)$) that at most $\lfloor \log_2 |U| \rfloor + 1$ candidate suffixes of any substring $U = S[l..r]$ can ever win under arbitrary right-extensions $T \in \Sigma^*$, compiling into $O(N)$ Segment Tree build via the 1-Survivor `pushup` theorem or $O(N)$-space Dyadic SA-Rank RMQ bands.
3. **[Chapter 07 — Lyndon Arrays ($\lambda_<, \lambda_>$), Double-Order Monotonic Stacks & Min-Cartesian Lyndon Tree Isomorphism](../chapters/ch07-lyndon-arrays-cartesian-trees.qmd)**: Identifying the longest Lyndon prefix starting at every index $i$ via the Next-Smaller-Suffix identity $R_{\mathcal{L}}[i] + 1 = \text{nsv}[i] = \min\{j > i \mid S[j..N] < S[i..N]\}$, constructing the Lyndon Tree of $\$S$ as the Min-Cartesian Tree of $\text{rk}[2..N+1]$ with left shift $[L_m - 1 .. R_m]$, and avoiding the $S = \texttt{bab}$ negated-rank trap on reversed order $>$.
4. **[Chapter 08 — The Runs Theorem (Bannai et al.), the Three-Squares Lemma & 2D Sweep-Line over Periodic Runs](../chapters/ch08-runs-theorem-squares-sweep.qmd)**: Seeding every maximal periodic substring $R = [l, r, p]$ ($\text{exp}(R) \ge 2$) from its disjoint interior $<_R$-Lyndon roots $B(R) \subseteq \{2, \dots, N\}$ to prove $|\mathcal{R}(S)| \le N - 1$, $\sum \text{exp}(R) < 3N$, and $< 2N$ canonical square representatives, then compiling substring repetition queries into 2D $(L, R)$-plane sweep-lines.

In a live contest, problem statements do not announce whether a lexicographical or periodic question belongs to `Ch 05`, `Ch 06`, `Ch 07`, or `Ch 08`. **Every visible problem statement in Section 2 is strictly unspoiled**: no chapter numbers or technique names appear outside the collapsible hints and solutions.

::: {.callout-important title="Zero-Spoiler Protocol & Progressive Hints"}
1. **Strict Zero-Spoiler Rule in Visible Statements**: Every problem statement (`CP-II-01` through `CP-II-07`) is written in pure contest form without naming the target chapter (`Ch 05`–`Ch 08`), Online Judge source, or technique (`Duval Automaton`, `CFL Block Greedy`, `Significant Suffixes`, `Dyadic SA-Rank RMQ`, `Lyndon Array`, `Runs Theorem`).
2. **Diagnose Before Peeking**: Before opening any dropdown on a problem, write down on scratch paper:
   - Which **Part II paradigm** (`Ch 05`–`Ch 08`) is triggered by the constraints and query geometry;
   - Which **lookalike decoy paradigm** must be ruled out, and why;
   - The **combinatorial word invariant** that collapses the naive $\Theta(N^2)$ or $\Theta(QN)$ bottleneck.
3. **Four-Stage Progressive Unmasking**:
   - **Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination**: Explains how to identify the governing paradigm and rule out lookalike decoys purely from constraints and query semantics.
   - **Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant**: States the exact CFL, tandem-annihilation, Lyndon-array, or periodic-run identity needed for the reduction.
   - **Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly**: Outlines the state representation, preprocessing structures, and complexity target.
   - **Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution**: Full proof, boundary pitfall audit, and complexity verification.
:::

## 1. Blind Diagnostic Triage Guide: Disambiguating Competing Part II Symptoms {#sec-cp02-triage-guide}

Before attempting the seven blind problems, study the two signature **Part II Decoy Pairs** below. Almost every misdiagnosis in Part II comes from confusing the two sides of one of these pairs.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Part II 4-Way Blind Triage Flowchart (Open After Reviewing Tables 1.1 & 1.2)"}

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    Q["Raw String Problem in Part II"] --> B1{"Lexicographical optimization\nor Periodic / Square structure?"}
    B1 -->|"Lexicographical / Suffix / Cyclic"| L1{"Fixed left endpoint l = 1\nwith empty extension T = ε?"}
    L1 -->|"Yes: Prefix S[1..r], T = ε\nor Global Cut / Shuffle"| C05["Ch 05: Duval Automaton\n• All-prefix min suffix: r -> r - d*p\n• All-prefix max suffix: outer pointer i under >\n• CFL block peeling / ω-order merge"]
    L1 -->|"No: Substring S[l..r] (l > 1)\nOR Right-Extension T ≠ ε"| C06["Ch 06: Significant Suffixes Cand(U)\n• |Cand(U)| <= floor(log2 |U|) + 1\n• Static T = ε min suffix: argmin rk + shortest border\n• General T ≠ ε or max suffix: 1-Survivor SegTree / Dyadic RMQ"]
    B1 -->|"Periodic / Lyndon Substrings / Squares"| P1{"Unbordered / Suffix-Dominance\nspans or Squares / Period >= 2?"}
    P1 -->|"Suffix-dominance S[i..r] < S[j..r]\nor Persistent Right-Spine"| C07["Ch 07: Lyndon Array & Lyndon Tree\n• nsv[i] = i + λ[i]\n• Min-Cartesian Tree of rk[2..N+1] -> S[L_m-1..R_m]\n• Guard: invert chars for >, NEVER negate rk_<"]
    P1 -->|"Squares w^2, k-th powers,\nSquare-free, or Borders >= |U|/2"| C08["Ch 08: Runs Theorem & 2D Sweep\n• |R(S)| < N, sum exp < 3N, < 2N rep squares\n• Clipping: min(R_q, r_R) - max(L_q, l_R) + 1 >= 2p\n• DSU skip-list or 2D Fenwick over (l_R, r_R, p)"]
```

### 1.1 Decoy Pair I: `Ch 05` All-Prefix CFL State Sharing vs. `Ch 06` Substring Significant Suffixes

| Diagnostic Dimension | `Ch 05` Symptom (Duval & All-Prefix CFL) | `Ch 06` Symptom (Significant Suffixes $\text{Cand}$) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Domain of Starting Indices $i$** | Prefix-global ($1 \le i \le r$) or whole-string block partition. | Arbitrary query range $l \le i \le r$ ($l > 1$), OR prefix $1 \le i \le r$ evaluated under a $r$-dependent right-extension $T_r \ne \varepsilon$. |
| **Right-Extension $T$** | Empty ($T = \varepsilon$) or infinite self-repetition $X^\omega$. | Non-empty $T \in \Sigma^+$ (e.g., cyclic shift $T = S[l..r]$, pattern $T = S[a..b]$, or Segment Tree right sibling $S[M+1..R]$). |
| **Why `Ch 05` Fails on `Ch 06`** | **Left-Truncation Non-Inclusion (`Counterexample 1`, `Ch 06 §4.3`)**: On $S = \texttt{aaba}$, $\text{Cand}_{\min}(S[1..4]) = \{\texttt{a}(4), \texttt{aaba}(1)\}$ kills $\texttt{aba}(2)$ because $\texttt{aaba} \prec \texttt{aba}$. When $l = 2$ cuts off index $1$, $\texttt{aba}(2)$ revives in $\text{Cand}_{\min}(S[2..4])$ and wins for $T = \texttt{c}$ ($\texttt{abac} < \texttt{ac}$). On $S = \texttt{abbb}, [l, r] = [2, 4]$, $\text{Cand}_{\min}(S[1..4]) \cap [2, 4] = \emptyset$. | **Overkill on $l = 1, T = \varepsilon$**: Maintaining $O(\log r)$ candidates with Z-array / LCE adds a $\log N$ factor where Duval's $r \to r - dp$ state sharing (`min_suf[r] = min_suf[r - d*p] + d*p`) or reversed-order outer pointer `max_suf[r] = i` runs in strict $O(1)$ amortized time and $O(1)$ auxiliary space. |
| **Tie-Break & Direction Asymmetry** | Under $<$, the last CFL factor $w_k$ is the **shortest** (= lexicographically smallest) suffix at $T = \varepsilon$. Under $>$, the last CFL factor is the shortest suffix in $>-$order, which **loses** to longer prefixes at $T = \varepsilon$; instead, Duval's outer pointer $i$ under $>$ gives the longest maximum suffix! | At $T = \varepsilon$, if $u \sqsubset v$, then $u < v$ always holds: **Minimum Suffix** favors the **shortest** border of $\arg\min_{i \in [l, r]} \text{rk}[i]$, whereas **Maximum Suffix** favors the **longest** surviving periodic extension $v$. Never append $+\infty$ to simulate $T = \varepsilon$ maximization! |

### 1.2 Decoy Pair II: `Ch 07` Lyndon Arrays & Cartesian Trees vs. `Ch 08` Periodic Runs & 2D Sweep-Lines

| Diagnostic Dimension | `Ch 07` Symptom (Lyndon Array & Lyndon Tree) | `Ch 08` Symptom (Runs $\mathcal{R}(S)$ & Representative Squares) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Core Structural Object** | Unbordered words $w \in \mathcal{L}$ satisfying $w \prec v$ for all proper suffixes $v$; laminar intervals $[i, R_{\mathcal{L}}[i]]$ where $R_{\mathcal{L}}[i] + 1 = \text{nsv}[i]$. | Maximal periodic intervals $R = [l_R, r_R, p]$ of primitive period $p$ and length $r_R - l_R + 1 \ge 2p$. |
| **How Lyndon Roots Bridge the Two** | Every right child $S[m..R_m]$ in the Lyndon Tree of $\$S$ (the Min-Cartesian Tree of $\text{rk}[2..N+1]$) is a right-maximal $<$-Lyndon word $[m, R_{\mathcal{L}, <}[m]]$. | Each run $R = [l_R, r_R, p]$ has $S[r_R+1] <_R S[r_R+1-p]$ for a unique order $<_R \in \{<, >\}$, which forces every $<_R$-Lyndon shift $i \in [l_R+1, r_R-p+1]$ inside $R$ to have $\lambda_{<_R}[i] = p$ and $S[i] <_R S[i-1]$. |
| **Signature Trap** | **The $S = \texttt{bab}$ Negated-Rank Trap**: Negating $-\text{rk}_<$ to simulate $>$ reverses proper-prefix order ($\texttt{bab} <_> \texttt{b}$) and falsely marks the bordered string $\texttt{bab}$ as Lyndon! Always invert characters $\overline{S}[t] = |\Sigma| + 1 - S[t]$ (keeping sentinel $0 = -\infty$) or check $j + \text{LCP}(i, j) > N$ in LCE. | **Harmonic & Multi-Run Deduplication Trap**: A run of period $p$ also generates non-primitive squares of half-length $d = kp$ ($k \ge 2$), and the **exact same square string $w^2$** can appear in multiple disjoint runs (e.g., $\texttt{ababxabab}$). Use the $< 2N$ canonical representatives $(R, k, a)$ plus SAM/SA deduplication! |

### Problem `CP-II-01` — Bounded-Cut Optional-Reversal Concatenation

> **Statement**: You are given a string $S[1..N]$ of lowercase English letters and an integer $K$ ($1 \le K \le N \le 5 \times 10^6$). You must partition $S$ into at most $K$ non-empty contiguous substrings
> $$S = P_1 P_2 \cdots P_m \qquad (1 \le m \le K),$$
> and for each piece $P_t$ independently choose either $P'_t = P_t$ (unreversed) or $P'_t = P_t^R$ (reversed). Find the lexicographically smallest string $P'_1 P'_2 \cdots P'_m$ obtainable over all valid partitions and reversal choices.
>
> **Constraints**: $1 \le K \le N \le 5 \times 10^6$, $|\Sigma| = 26$, time limit $2.0\text{ s}$, memory limit $256\text{ MB}$. Because $N = 5 \times 10^6$, your algorithm must run in **strict $O(N)$ time**.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}
- **Decoy Elimination**: With $N = 5 \times 10^6$ and a $2.0\text{ s}$ time limit, $O(N \log N)$ Suffix Array or Significant Suffix Segment Tree methods (`Ch 06`) cannot fit in time or memory; we need a strictly $O(N)$-time global prefix/suffix decomposition (`Ch 05`).
- **Diagnostic Signal**: Reversing a prefix $P_1 = S[1..i]$ and placing it at the front of the output is identical to detaching the **suffix** $T[N-i+1..N]$ of the reversed string $T = S^R$ and placing it at the front. If you are allowed to detach a suffix of $T$ to form the prefix of your answer, which suffix of $T$ begins with the lexicographically smallest possible characters? Which Part II chapter characterizes the lexicographically smallest suffix of a string and its repeating blocks in $O(N)$ time?
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}
**Block Coalescing & Unary Runs**: In the Chen–Fox–Lyndon factorization of the reversed string $T = S^R = w_1^{d_1} w_2^{d_2} \cdots w_r^{d_r}$ with $w_1 > w_2 > \cdots > w_r$:

1. By CFL uniqueness (`Ch 05`), $w_r$ is the lexicographically smallest nonempty suffix of $T$, and detaching the entire equal-factor power block $B_r = w_r^{d_r}$ from the end of $T$ corresponds to reversing a single prefix of $S$ (consuming just **1 cut**!).
2. What if $|w_r| = |w_{r-1}| = 1$ (e.g., $T$ ends with $\texttt{c}\texttt{b}\texttt{a}$, so $S$ starts with $\texttt{a}\texttt{b}\texttt{c}$)? Reversing a $1$-character piece does nothing! Adjacent blocks $B_t$ of factor length $|w_t| = 1$ can all be left **unreversed** as a single contiguous prefix of $S$, consuming only **1 cut** in total!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}
**The $K = 2$ Border Trap**: Greedily peel the last CFL block $B_r = w_r^{d_r}$ from $T = S^R$ (merging consecutive $|w_t| = 1$ blocks into a single cut) while the remaining cut budget satisfies $k \ge 3$. When $k = 2$ cuts remain on the remaining prefix $S'[1..m]$ ($T' = (S')^R$), you must choose the lexicographical minimum of **four** $O(m)$ candidates:

1. **1-Piece**: $\min(S', T')$.
2. **Reversed Prefix + Unreversed Suffix**: $\min_{1 \le i < m} \bigl((S'[1..i])^R + S'[i+1..m]\bigr)$. Since $(S'[1..i])^R$ is a suffix of $T'$, this asks for a suffix of $T'$ followed by a complementary suffix of $S'$—or notice that in the unreversed-prefix + reversed-suffix case below, we detach a suffix of $T'$! Wait: for $(S'[1..i])^R + S'[i+1..m]$, this is equivalent to reversing a prefix $S'[1..i]$ and leaving $S'[i+1..m]$ unreversed, which is detaching a suffix $T'[m-i+1..m]$ of $T'$ and appending $(T'[1..m-i])^R$! By CFL theory on $T'$, only two suffix boundaries of $T'$ can ever win when right-extended: cutting after the last CFL block $B_r$, or (when $B_r \sqsubset B_{r-1}$) cutting after $B_{r-1} B_r$!
3. **Unreversed Prefix + Reversed Suffix**: $\min_{1 \le i < m} \bigl(S'[1..i] + (S'[i+1..m])^R\bigr) = \min_{1 \le i < m} \bigl(S'[1..i] + T'[1..m-i]\bigr)$. Notice that for every $i$, $S'[1..i] + T'[1..m-i]$ starts with a prefix of $S'$ followed by a prefix of $T'$; comparing any two cut points $i < j$ reduces to a single $O(1)$ Z-array lookup on $T'$ and $T' + S'$!
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-II-01"}
#### 1. Target Paradigm & Diagnostic Breakdown

- **Source / Origin**: Codeforces 594E — *Cutting the Line* (`W1B-11`).
- **Target Chapter**: `Ch 05` (Duval's $O(N)$ CFL Automaton & CFL Block Greedy) coupled with $O(N)$ Z-array LCE comparisons for the $k = 2$ boundary cases.
- **Why $O(N \log N)$ Suffix Arrays Fail**: With $N = 5 \times 10^6$ and a $2.0\text{ s}$ limit, only linear-time primitives (Duval's algorithm and the Z-algorithm) fit within time and memory.

#### 2. Mathematical Derivation of the $k \ge 3$ Greedy Invariant
Let $T = S^R = w_1^{d_1} w_2^{d_2} \cdots w_r^{d_r}$ ($w_1 > w_2 > \cdots > w_r$, $w_t \in \mathcal{L}$) be the compressed CFL factorization of $S^R$, where $B_t = w_t^{d_t}$.

- Every piece $P_1 = S[1..i]$ reversed at the front of the output equals the suffix $T[N-i+1..N]$ of $T$.
- By Theorem 5.2(2) of `Ch 05`, $w_r$ is the lexicographically smallest nonempty suffix of $T$, and because $w_r \in \mathcal{L}$ is border-free, any suffix of $T$ that is not of the form $w_r^c$ ($1 \le c \le d_r$) is strictly larger than $w_r$ at a character mismatch before $|w_r|$ ($\prec$).
- Moreover, why should we detach the **entire** block $B_r = w_r^{d_r}$ rather than stopping at $w_r^c$ ($c < d_r$) when $k \ge 3$? Because if we stopped at $w_r^c$, the remaining string $T[1..N - c|w_r|]$ would still end with $w_r^{d_r - c}$, which is strictly smaller than every other suffix of the remainder! With $k \ge 3$, we could spend our next cut to detach $w_r^{d_r - c}$ immediately afterward, producing the exact same prefix $w_r^{d_r}$ at the cost of two cuts instead of one.
- **The Unary Block Coalescing Rule**: If $|w_r| = 1$, reversing a single character is a no-op. If several consecutive blocks at the end of $T$ have $|w_r| = |w_{r-1}| = \cdots = |w_{r-s}| = 1$ (say $T$ ends with $c_1^{d_{r-s}} \cdots c_{s+1}^{d_r}$ where $c_1 > \cdots > c_{s+1}$), then in $S = T^R$ those blocks form the prefix $c_{s+1}^{d_r} \cdots c_1^{d_{r-s}}$ in **already sorted order** without reversing! Thus we can peel all consecutive $|w_t| = 1$ blocks at the end of $T$ while charging only **1 cut** for the entire unary run.

#### 3. Exact Analysis of the $k = 2$ Base Case on Remaining $S'[1..m]$ ($T' = (S')^R$)
When $k = 1$, no more cuts can be made inside $S'[1..m]$: we simply append $\min(S', T')$.
When $k = 2$ (meaning we may split $S'[1..m]$ into at most $2$ pieces), there are four cases for $P'_1 P'_2$:

1. **Case A ($1$ piece, unreversed or reversed)**: Candidate is $\min(S', T')$.
2. **Case B ($P'_1 = (S'[1..i])^R, P'_2 = (S'[i+1..m])^R$)**: Notice $(S'[1..i])^R + (S'[i+1..m])^R$ is a 2-cut candidate, which is always $\ge$ detaching $B_r$ and reversing the rest (already covered by peeling one more step to $k=1$).
3. **Case C ($P'_1 = (S'[1..i])^R, P'_2 = S'[i+1..m]$ — Reversed Prefix + Unreversed Suffix)**:
   Here $P'_1 = T'[m-i+1..m]$ is a suffix of $T'$, and $P'_2 = (T'[1..m-i])^R$. By Theorem 6.2 (`Ch 06` Significant Suffixes) and CFL structure on $T' = B_1 B_2 \cdots B_q$:

   - Any suffix of $T'$ not equal to a suffix of $B_q = w_q^{d_q}$ (or a suffix $B_{t} \cdots B_q$ that has $B_q$ as a proper prefix) loses via strong inequality $\prec$ before reaching $P'_2$.
   - Inside a single block $B_q = w_q^{d_q}$, taking the full block $B_q$ always beats a partial copy $w_q^c$ ($c < d_q$) because the next character of $P'_2 = (T'[1..m-c|w_q|])^R$ would start with the first character of $T'$ (or we can simply note that $B_q$ is a prefix of $B_{q-1}$ only if $w_q \sqsubset w_{q-1}$).
   - In fact, by CFL dominance (`Ch 05`), the optimal suffix of $T'$ in Case C is **either $B_q$ or $B_{q-1} B_q$**! Comparing just these two strings of length $m$ takes $O(m)$ time.
4. **Case D ($P'_1 = S'[1..i], P'_2 = (S'[i+1..m])^R = T'[1..m-i]$ — Unreversed Prefix + Reversed Suffix)**:
   For $1 \le i < j \le m$, compare $C(i) = S'[1..i] + T'[1..m-i]$ against $C(j) = S'[1..j] + T'[1..m-j]$:

   - Both share the prefix $S'[1..i]$.
   - Next, compare $T'[1..j-i]$ (from $C(i)$) against $S'[i+1..j]$ (from $C(j)$) using one $O(1)$ Z-array lookup on $Z_{T' + S'}[m + i + 1]$.
   - If they match all $j - i$ characters, compare $T'[j-i+1..m-i]$ (from $C(i)$) against $T'[1..m-j]$ (from $C(j)$) using one $O(1)$ Z-array lookup on $Z_{T'}[j - i + 1]$.
   Maintaining the running best $i^* \in [1, m-1]$ takes $O(m)$ time.

#### 4. Complexity & Pitfall Audit

- **Time Complexity**: $O(N)$ for Duval on $T = S^R$, $O(m) \le O(N)$ for the Z-arrays on $T' + S'$ and the 4-way comparison at $k = 2$. Total time: $O(N)$, auxiliary space: $O(N)$.
- **Pitfall Guard**: Never charge a new cut when transitioning from a $|w_t| = 1$ CFL block to an adjacent $|w_{t-1}| = 1$ CFL block; only charge a cut when the state switches out of the unary unreversed run.
::::

### Problem `CP-II-02` — Minimum-Rank Two-String Interleaving & Block Shuffle

> **Statement**: You are given two strings $A[1..N]$ and $B[1..M]$ ($1 \le N, M \le 2 \times 10^5$) over an ordered alphabet $\Sigma = \{1, \dots, \sigma\}$ ($\sigma \le 2 \times 10^5$). An **interleaving (shuffle)** of $A$ and $B$ is any string $C[1..N+M]$ formed by partitioning the indices $\{1, \dots, N+M\}$ into two subsequences of lengths $N$ and $M$ equal to $A$ and $B$ respectively.
>
> Solve both variants of the problem in $O(N + M)$ time:
>
> 1. **Character-Level Shuffle**: Find the lexicographically smallest interleaving $C_{\min}[1..N+M]$ of $A$ and $B$.
> 2. **Atomic-Block Decomposition**: Prove that $A = u_1 u_2 \cdots u_p$ and $B = v_1 v_2 \cdots v_q$ each admit a canonical factorization into contiguous blocks such that for **every** pair of strings $A, B$, $C_{\min}$ is obtained by merging the two block sequences $(u_1, \dots, u_p)$ and $(v_1, \dots, v_q)$ in sorted order without ever splitting a block, and output the block boundaries $(|u_1|, \dots, |u_p|)$ and $(|v_1|, \dots, |v_q|)$.
>
> **Constraints**: $1 \le N, M \le 2 \times 10^5$, $\sigma \le 2 \times 10^5$, time limit $1.5\text{ s}$, memory limit $256\text{ MB}$.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}
- **Decoy Elimination**: Standard suffix comparison with $-\infty$ (`$`) sentinels fails at proper-prefix ties! Suppose $A[i..N] = \texttt{ba}$ and $B[j..M] = \texttt{baa}$: standard suffix order says $\texttt{ba} < \texttt{baa}$, which would exhaust $A$ first and produce $A + B = \texttt{babaa} > \texttt{baaba} = B + A$.
- **Diagnostic Signal**: When merging $A[i..N]$ and $B[j..M]$ to minimize $C$, exhausting $A[i..N]$ early exposes the remainder of $B$, which is equivalent to comparing $A[i..N] + (+\infty)$ against $B[j..M] + (+\infty)$. Which Part II canonical factorization decomposes $A$ and $B$ into atomic blocks that never split during a minimum-rank merge?
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}
**Reversed-Order CFL Factorization**: Suppose a contiguous block $u$ of $A$ satisfies the property that every nonempty proper suffix $s$ of $u$ is **strictly smaller** than $u$ in standard order $<$ (and does not have $u$ as a prefix—i.e., $u$ is a **Lyndon word under the reversed alphabet order $>$**!). Once you choose the first character $u[1]$ of $u$ over the current head of $B$, every subsequent suffix $s$ of $u$ satisfies $s <_< u$, so $u$ will continue beating the head of $B$ uninterrupted until the entire block $u$ is emitted!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}

1. Factor $A = u_1 u_2 \cdots u_p$ and $B = v_1 v_2 \cdots v_q$ using Duval's algorithm under the **reversed alphabet order $>$** (`Ch 05`).
2. Why does a $>-$CFL factorization satisfy $u_1 \le_< u_2 \le_< \cdots \le_< u_p$ when viewed in standard order $<$ (with $+\infty$ appended)? Because in $>-$order, $u_1 \ge_> u_2 \ge_> \cdots \ge_> u_p$, and if $u_t$ is not a prefix of $u_{t+1}$, reversing the alphabet flips $>$ to $<$; if $u_{t+1} \sqsubset u_t$, write $u_t = u_{t+1} s$, and since $u_t$ is $>-$Lyndon, $s >_> u_t \implies s <_< u_t$, so $u_t$ is smaller than $u_{t+1}$ under $\omega$-order $u_t^\omega \le_< u_{t+1}^\omega$!
3. Thus merging $(u_1, \dots, u_p)$ and $(v_1, \dots, v_q)$ by infinite periodic order $X^\omega \le_< Y^\omega$ (or equivalently, building a linear-time Suffix Array on $A + (+\infty_1) + B + (+\infty_2)$ where $+\infty_1, +\infty_2 > \max \Sigma$) produces $C_{\min}$ in $O(N + M)$ time!
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-II-02"}
#### 1. Target Paradigm & Diagnostic Breakdown

- **Source / Origin**: Codeforces 1906I / ICPC World Finals & Lothaire's Shuffle Synthesis (`W1B-32`).
- **Target Chapter**: `Ch 05` (Duval's Automaton under Reversed Order $>$ & $\omega$-Order Concatenation) / Lothaire's CFL Shuffle Theorem.
- **Core Trap**: Standard Suffix Array building appends $-\infty$ (`$`), which makes a shorter prefix $X \sqsubset Y$ smaller than $Y$. When minimizing a merge/interleaving, exhausting $X$ exposes the remainder of $Y$, whereas advancing $Y$ exposes $Y[|X|+1..]$.

#### 2. Proof of Lothaire's Reversed-Order CFL Shuffle Theorem
Let $<_R$ denote the reversed alphabet order ($a <_R b \iff a > b$ on characters of $\Sigma$). Factor $A$ and $B$ into their unique Chen–Fox–Lyndon factorizations under $<_R$:
$$A = u_1 u_2 \cdots u_p \quad (u_1 \ge_R \cdots \ge_R u_p), \qquad B = v_1 v_2 \cdots v_q \quad (v_1 \ge_R \cdots \ge_R v_q).$$
We prove two facts:

1. **Each $<_R$-Lyndon factor $u_t$ is Atomic (Never Split in $C_{\min}$)**:
   For any nonempty proper suffix $s$ of $u_t$, Theorem 5.1(3) applied to $<_R$ states that $u_t \prec_R s$, meaning $u_t$ and $s$ mismatch at some character position $\le |s|$ where $u_t$ is larger in $<$, i.e.,
   $$s \prec_< u_t \qquad (\text{in standard order } <\text{!}).$$
   Furthermore, in infinite periodic order under $<$, $s^\omega <_< u_t^\omega$. Therefore, once $u_t$ is at the head of $A$ and beats $v_r$ ($u_t^\omega \le_< v_r^\omega$), every proper suffix $s$ of $u_t$ reached after emitting the first character of $u_t$ satisfies $s^\omega <_< u_t^\omega \le_< v_r^\omega$, so $s$ **strictly beats $v_r$** until all of $u_t$ is emitted!

2. **Monotonicity of Factors Under $<_\omega$**:
   In the $<_R$-CFL factorization $u_1 \ge_R u_2 \ge_R \cdots \ge_R u_p$:

   - If $u_t = u_{t+1}$, then $u_t^\omega = u_{t+1}^\omega$.
   - If $u_t \succ_R u_{t+1}$ (mismatch within $\min(|u_t|, |u_{t+1}|)$), then in standard order $u_t \prec_< u_{t+1}$, so $u_t^\omega <_< u_{t+1}^\omega$.
   - If $u_{t+1} \sqsubset u_t$, write $u_t = u_{t+1}^d w' s$ where $u_t \in \mathcal{L}_{<_R}$ forces the suffix after $u_{t+1}$ to satisfy $s \prec_< u_t$, yielding $u_t^\omega <_< u_{t+1}^\omega$.
   Thus in standard periodic order $<_\omega$, the factors of $A$ and $B$ already satisfy:
   $$u_1^\omega \le_< u_2^\omega \le_< \cdots \le_< u_p^\omega, \qquad v_1^\omega \le_< v_2^\omega \le_< \cdots \le_< v_q^\omega!$$

Consequently, $C_{\min}$ is obtained simply by running a standard two-pointer merge on the sorted factor lists $(u_1, \dots, u_p)$ and $(v_1, \dots, v_q)$ under $u_i^\omega \le_< v_j^\omega$!

#### 3. $O(N + M)$ Algorithmic Contract

1. **Atomic Block Boundaries**: Run Duval's algorithm on $A$ and on $B$ using the reversed character comparator `a > b` in $< 2(N + M)$ character comparisons to emit $(|u_1|, \dots, |u_p|)$ and $(|v_1|, \dots, |v_q|)$.
2. **Two-Pointer Merge via $+\infty$ Suffix Ranks**: Alternatively (or to compare $u_i^\omega$ vs $v_j^\omega$ in $O(1)$), construct the Suffix Array of
   $$W = A + (\sigma + 1) + B + (\sigma + 2)$$
   in $O(N + M)$ time, where $\sigma + 1 < \sigma + 2$ are two distinct $+\infty$ sentinels strictly larger than all characters in $\Sigma$. At each step, compare $\text{rk}_W[\text{head}(A)]$ vs $\text{rk}_W[N + 1 + \text{head}(B)]$ in $O(1)$ time and advance the smaller pointer.

   - *Why $+\infty$ Sentinels Match $u_i^\omega \le_< v_j^\omega$*: Because every remaining suffix $A[\text{head}(A)..N]$ starts with $u_i \le_\omega u_{i+1} \le_\omega \cdots \le_\omega u_p <_\omega +\infty$, if $A[\text{head}(A)..N]$ is a proper prefix of $B[\text{head}(B)..M]$, the $+\infty$ sentinel after $A$ is strictly larger than the next character of $B$, forcing the merge to advance $B$ first—exactly matching the periodic block comparison!
::::

### Problem `CP-II-03` — Sub-Linear-Node Memory Substring Suffix & Prefix-Rotation Queries

> **Statement**: You are given a static string $S[1..N]$ ($1 \le N \le 3 \times 10^5$) over lowercase English letters and $Q$ online queries ($1 \le Q \le 3 \times 10^5$). Each query provides an interval $[l, r]$ ($1 \le l \le r \le N$) and asks for two indices $(i_{\min}, i_{\max}) \in [l, r]^2$:
>
> 1. **$i_{\min}$**: The starting index $i \in [l, r]$ that lexicographically minimizes the concatenated string $S[i..r] + S[1..l-1]$ (if $l = 1$, $S[1..0] = \varepsilon$; break ties by **smallest** starting index $i$).
> 2. **$i_{\max}$**: The starting index $i \in [l, r]$ that lexicographically maximizes the suffix $S[i..r]$ of $S[l..r]$.
>
> **Constraints**: $1 \le N, Q \le 3 \times 10^5$, time limit $2.0\text{ s}$, **strict memory limit $48\text{ MB}$** (forbidding $O(N \log N)$-space node/vector trees).

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}
- **Decoy Elimination (Decoy Pair I)**: Because queries ask for suffixes of an arbitrary substring $S[l..r]$ ($l > 1$)—with a non-empty right-extension $T = S[1..l-1]$ in Part 1 and maximization at $T = \varepsilon$ in Part 2—`Ch 05`'s prefix-global Duval state sharing (`Counterexample 1`: $S = \texttt{aaba}, [l, r] = [2, 4]$) fails completely.
- **Diagnostic Signal**: By `Ch 06` (`Theorem 6.2`), both answers must belong to the Significant Suffix set $\text{Cand}(S[l..r])$ of size $\le \lfloor \log_2(r - l + 1) \rfloor + 1$. However, the $48\text{ MB}$ memory limit forbids building a Segment Tree of $\text{Cand}([L, R])$. How can we extract a superset of $\text{Cand}(S[l..r])$ of size $O(\log(r - l + 1))$ on the fly using **only** RMQ queries on $\text{rk}[1..N]$?
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}
**Dyadic SA-Rank RMQ Bands & Periodic Left-Shift**: Partition the suffix lengths $[1, r - l + 1]$ into $K = \lfloor \log_2(r - l + 1) \rfloor + 1$ dyadic bands $B_k = [2^k, \min(r - l + 1, 2^{k+1} - 1)]$, corresponding to starting-index intervals $I_k = [\max(l, r - 2^{k+1} + 2),\; r - 2^k + 1]$.

1. By Theorem 6.2 (`Ch 06`), at most **one** suffix in each band $I_k$ can belong to $\text{Cand}_{\min}(S[l..r])$ (and similarly for $\text{Cand}_{\max}(S[l..r])$).
2. In band $I_k$, let $i_k = \arg\min_{x \in I_k} \text{rk}[x]$. Any $x \in I_k$ that mismatches $S[i_k..r]$ before $r$ is strictly larger than $S[i_k..r]$ for **every** right-extension $T$!
3. When can the true survivor $x^* \in \text{Cand}_{\min}(S[l..r]) \cap I_k$ differ from $i_k$? Only when $x^* < i_k$ in $I_k$ and $S[i_k..r] \sqsubset S[x^*..r]$ (no mismatch before $r$). By Tandem Annihilation (`Theorem 6.2`), only the **longest** periodic copy $x^*$ in $I_k$ can survive!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}
**Recovering $x^*$ in $O(1)$ per Band**: For **Part 2 ($i_{\max}$, Substring Maximum Suffix at $T = \varepsilon$)**:

- Let $j_0 = \arg\max_{x \in [l, r]} \text{rk}[x]$ (a single RMQ query on $\text{rk}$!). Any $x \in [l, r]$ that mismatches $S[j_0..r]$ before $r$ has $\text{rk}[x] < \text{rk}[j_0]$ and therefore loses to $S[j_0..r]$ at that mismatch!
- Could some $x \in [l, r]$ match $S[j_0..r]$ without mismatch before $r$ and beat $S[j_0..r]$ at $T = \varepsilon$? To beat $S[j_0..r]$ at $T = \varepsilon$ without mismatching before $r$, $S[x..r]$ must be **strictly longer** than $S[j_0..r]$ ($x < j_0$) and have $S[j_0..r] \sqsubset S[x..r]$!
- Thus $i_{\max}$ is simply the **earliest** index $x \in \text{Cand}_{\max}(S[l..r])$ that wins at $T = \varepsilon$, which we find in $O(\log(r - l + 1))$ time by querying $j_k = \arg\max_{x \in I_k} \text{rk}[x]$ in each dyadic band $I_k$ (plus shifting $j_k$ left to the earliest periodic copy in $I_k$ if $S[j_k..r]$ has period $p \le |S[j_k..r]|/2$, or simply noting that if $x^* < j_k$ in $I_k$ has $S[j_k..r] \sqsubset S[x^*..r]$, then $p = j_k - x^* < |S[j_k..r]|$, and at index $r + 1$, $S[r + 1 - p] > S[r + 1]$!).
- And how do we find the period $p$ of $S[i_k..r]$ (or $S[j_k..r]$) in $O(1)$ time if a longer periodic extension $x^* \in I_k$ exists? Query the primary RMQ winner $i_1 = \arg\min_{x \in I_k} \text{rk}[x]$ and the secondary RMQ winner strictly to its left $i_2 = \arg\min_{x \in [l_k, i_1 - 1]} \text{rk}[x]$. If $\text{LCP}(i_1, i_2) \ge r - i_1 + 1$, then $p = i_1 - i_2$ is the exact period, and a single reverse-LCE query $\text{LCS}(i_2, i_1)$ jumps directly to the earliest full period shift $x^*_k$ in $I_k$!
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-II-03"}
#### 1. Target Paradigm & Diagnostic Breakdown

- **Source / Origin**: Synthesis of Kociumaka et al. (2014) Dyadic Bands, `[JSOI2019]` & `[ZJOI2017]` Static Core (`W1B-25` / `W1B-26`).
- **Target Chapter**: `Ch 06` (`§6.4` Segment-Tree-Free Dyadic SA-Rank RMQ Band Extraction of $\text{Cand}_{\min/\max}(S[l..r])$).
- **Why Standard `Ch 05` or $T = \varepsilon$ Shortcuts Fail**:
  1. For Part 1 ($i_{\min}$ minimizing $S[i..r] + S[1..l-1]$), the right-extension $T = S[1..l-1]$ is non-empty for $l > 1$, and ties are broken by **smallest $i$** (longest suffix $S[i..r]$).
  2. For Part 2 ($i_{\max}$ maximizing $S[i..r]$), at $T = \varepsilon$, if $u \sqsubset v$, the **longer** suffix $v$ beats $u$ ($v > u$). Yet in the global Suffix Array $\text{rk}$, $S[r+1..N]$ follows both $u$ and $v$; if $S[r+1] < S[r+1-(|v|-|u|)]$, then globally $\text{rk}[i_v] < \text{rk}[i_u]$, so $j_0 = \arg\max_{x \in [l, r]} \text{rk}[x]$ picks the **shorter** copy $u$ instead of the true winner $v$!

#### 2. Exact $O(1)$-Per-Band Recovery of the Unique Survivor $x^*_k \in I_k$
Fix a query $[l, r]$ and a dyadic band $k \in [0, \lfloor \log_2(r - l + 1) \rfloor]$ with length range $B_k = [2^k, \min(r - l + 1, 2^{k+1} - 1)]$ and start-index interval
$$I_k = \bigl[\max(l, r - 2^{k+1} + 2),\; r - 2^k + 1\bigr].$$
Let us extract the unique potential survivor $x^{\min}_k \in I_k$ for $\text{Cand}_{\min}(S[l..r])$ (and identically $x^{\max}_k \in I_k$ for $\text{Cand}_{\max}(S[l..r])$):

1. Query the primary RMQ winner $i_1 = \arg\min_{x \in I_k} \text{rk}[x]$ in $O(1)$ time.
2. Could the true survivor $x^* \in I_k$ satisfy $x^* < i_1$ with $S[i_1..r] \sqsubset S[x^*..r]$?
   - If so, no character mismatch occurs between $S[x^*..r]$ and $S[i_1..r]$ before $r$. What about any other index $y \in [l_k, i_1 - 1]$ ($l_k = \max(l, r - 2^{k+1} + 2)$)?
   - Query the secondary RMQ winner strictly to the left of $i_1$:
     $$i_2 = \arg\min_{x \in [l_k, i_1 - 1]} \text{rk}[x].$$

   - **Lemma (Two-RMQ Period Pinning)**: If there exists *any* $x \in [l_k, i_1 - 1]$ such that $S[i_1..r] \sqsubset S[x..r]$, then $i_2 = \arg\min_{x \in [l_k, i_1 - 1]} \text{rk}[x]$ **must also satisfy $S[i_1..r] \sqsubset S[i_2..r]$**!
     *Proof*: Why? Because $S[i_1..r]$ is already the lexicographically smallest substring of length $r - i_1 + 1$ among all starting positions in $I_k$ (since $i_1$ minimizes $\text{rk}$ on all of $I_k$). Therefore, any $y \in [l_k, i_1 - 1]$ that does *not* have $S[i_1..r]$ as a prefix must mismatch $S[i_1..r]$ before $r$ with a **larger** character, which means $\text{rk}[y] > \text{rk}[x]$ for every $x \in [l_k, i_1 - 1]$ that *does* share the prefix $S[i_1..r]$! Hence the minimum-rank index $i_2 \in [l_k, i_1 - 1]$ is guaranteed to share the prefix $S[i_1..r]$!

   - Furthermore, among all $x \in [l_k, i_1 - 1]$ satisfying $S[i_1..r] \sqsubset S[x..r]$, they are all prefixes of the same periodic run of period $p = \gcd\text{-period}$, and by Tandem Annihilation (`Theorem 6.2`), at every step along the period progression $i_1, i_1 - p, i_1 - 2p, \dots$, the global suffixes $S[i_1 - tp .. N]$ are **strictly monotonic** in $\text{rk}$ (specifically, since $\text{rk}[i_1] < \text{rk}[i_1 - p]$, left-cancelling $w$ proves $\text{rk}[i_1] < \text{rk}[i_1 - p] < \text{rk}[i_1 - 2p] < \cdots$!).
   - **Look at what $\text{rk}[i_1] < \text{rk}[i_1 - p] < \text{rk}[i_1 - 2p] < \cdots$ means**:
     The minimum-rank index $i_2 = \arg\min_{x \in [l_k, i_1 - 1]} \text{rk}[x]$ is **literally the very first periodic shift $i_1 - p$**!

3. Therefore, in **two $O(1)$ RMQ queries** ($i_1$ on $I_k$, and $i_2$ on $[l_k, i_1 - 1]$):
   - Check if $\text{LCP}(i_1, i_2) \ge r - i_1 + 1$.
   - If **No**, then no $x \in [l_k, i_1 - 1]$ has $S[i_1..r]$ as a prefix, so $x^*_k = i_1$!
   - If **Yes**, then $p = i_1 - i_2$ is the exact period! Find how far the period $p$ extends to the left of $i_1$ inside $I_k$ via a single reverse-LCE query $L_{\text{left}} = \text{LCS}(i_1 - 1, i_1 + p - 1)$ (or $\text{LCP}(\max(l_k, i_1 - L_{\text{left}}), \dots)$), and jump directly to the earliest full period shift:
     $$x^*_k = i_1 - \left\lfloor \frac{\min(i_1 - l_k, \text{LCS}(i_2, i_1))}{p} \right\rfloor \cdot p!$$
   The exact same logic (replacing $\arg\min \text{rk}$ with $\arg\max \text{rk}$) recovers the unique band representative $x^{\max}_k \in I_k$ for $\text{Cand}_{\max}(S[l..r])$ in $O(1)$ time!

#### 3. Evaluating $i_{\min}$ and $i_{\max}$ Across the $\le 19$ Band Representatives

- **For $i_{\max}$ ($T = \varepsilon$)**: Compare the $\le 19$ representatives $x^{\max}_k$ ($k = 0 \dots \lfloor \log_2(r-l+1) \rfloor$) using $O(1)$ LCE (`LCP`): for $a < b$, if $\text{LCP}(a, b) \ge r - b + 1$, the longer suffix $a$ wins ($S[a..r] > S[b..r]$); otherwise compare $\text{rk}[a]$ vs $\text{rk}[b]$.
- **For $i_{\min}$ ($T = S[1..l-1]$, tie-break by smallest $i$)**: Compare the $\le 19$ representatives $x^{\min}_k$ using at most **two $O(1)$ LCE queries** per comparison: to compare $S[a..r] + S[1..l-1]$ vs $S[b..r] + S[1..l-1]$ ($a < b$), first compare $S[a..r]$ vs $S[b..r]$ (length $r - b + 1$), then $S[a + (r - b + 1)..r]$ vs $S[1..l-1]$, then $S[1..l-1]$ vs $S[1 + (b - a)..l-1]$. On an exact tie of length $(r - a + 1) + (l - 1)$, the longer suffix $a < b$ automatically wins!

#### 4. Complexity & Memory Verification

- **Space**: Only `SA`, `rk`, `height`, and a single RMQ sparse table on `height` and `rk` (or block-RMQ) — $< 35\text{ MB}$ for $N = 3 \times 10^5$.
- **Time**: $O(N \log N)$ preprocessing, $O(\log(r - l + 1))$ per query with tiny constant factor ($\le 38$ RMQ lookups per query).

### Problem `CP-II-04` — Inverse Suffix-Dominance Span Reconstruction

> **Statement**: For an unknown string $S[1..N]$ ($1 \le N \le 5 \times 10^5$) over a totally ordered integer alphabet $\{1, 2, \dots, \sigma\}$, an oracle records for every starting position $i \in [1, N]$ the integer $\ell_i \ge 1$ defined as the length of the **longest prefix $S[i..i+\ell_i-1]$ of $S[i..N]$ that is strictly lexicographically smaller than every one of its own nonempty proper suffixes**.
>
> Given only the array $\ell_1, \ell_2, \dots, \ell_N$ ($1 \le \ell_i \le N - i + 1$):
>
> 1. Determine whether there exists at least one valid string $S[1..N]$ over some ordered alphabet whose oracle array equals $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_N$.
> 2. If valid, find the **minimum possible alphabet size $\sigma_{\min}$** and construct the **lexicographically smallest** valid string $S[1..N] \in \{1, \dots, \sigma_{\min}\}^N$ (or output `-1` if no such string exists).
>
> **Constraints**: $1 \le N \le 5 \times 10^5$, $1 \le \ell_i \le N - i + 1$, time limit $1.5\text{ s}$, memory limit $256\text{ MB}$.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}
- **Decoy Elimination (Decoy Pair II)**: The oracle does not count periodic squares (`Ch 08`) or right-extended suffix candidates (`Ch 06`); it records at every index $i$ the longest prefix of $S[i..N]$ that is strictly smaller than all of its own proper suffixes.
- **Diagnostic Signal**: What is a word $w$ that is "strictly lexicographically smaller than every one of its own nonempty proper suffixes"? By Theorem 5.1(2) of `Ch 05`, that is the exact definition of a **Lyndon word** ($w \in \mathcal{L}$)! Thus $\ell_i = \lambda[i]$ is the **Lyndon Array** of $S[1..N]$ (`Ch 07`), and $R_{\mathcal{L}}[i] = i + \ell_i - 1$ is the right endpoint of the longest Lyndon prefix starting at $i$.
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}
**Next-Smaller-Suffix & Laminar Family**: By the Next-Smaller-Suffix Identity (`Ch 07`, `Theorem 7.1`), with $S[N+1..N] = \varepsilon = -\infty$:
$$\text{nsv}[i] = i + \ell_i = \min \bigl\{ j \in [i+1, N+1] \;\big|\; S[j..N] < S[i..N] \bigr\}.$$

1. **Necessary Laminar Condition**: Can two intervals $[i, i + \ell_i - 1]$ and $[j, j + \ell_j - 1]$ with $i < j \le i + \ell_i - 1$ ever satisfy $j + \ell_j > i + \ell_i$? No! Because for $j \in [i+1, i+\ell_i-1]$, $\text{nsv}[i] = i + \ell_i$ means $S[k..N] > S[i..N]$ for all $k \in [i+1, i+\ell_i-1]$ while $S[i+\ell_i..N] < S[i..N] < S[j..N]$, which forces $\text{nsv}[j] \le i + \ell_i$!
2. Once the intervals $[i, i + \ell_i - 1]$ are verified to be **laminar** (nested or disjoint), how do we assign a canonical Suffix Array permutation $\text{SA}[1..N]$?
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}

1. Build the rooted tree on vertices $\{1, \dots, N+1\}$ with parent edges $i \to \text{nsv}[i] = i + \ell_i$ (rooted at $N + 1$). Verify laminar nesting in $O(N)$ using a stack: when scanning $i = 1 \to N$, $i + \ell_i$ must never exceed the current enclosing parent on the stack.
2. In this Next-Smaller-Element tree, $\text{nsv}[i] = p$ requires:
   - $S[p..N] < S[i..N]$ (every child $i$ has strictly **larger** suffix rank than its parent $p$), and
   - For two siblings $i_1 < i_2$ sharing parent $p$, $i_2 \in [i_1 + 1, p - 1]$ implies $S[i_1..N] < S[i_2..N]$!
   Thus an in-order / pre-order traversal that visits each vertex $p$ **before** its children, and visits the children $i_1 < i_2 < \cdots < i_k$ of $p$ in **increasing order of index**, puts $\text{rk}[p] < \text{rk}[\text{subtree}(i_1)] < \text{rk}[\text{subtree}(i_2)] < \cdots$, which guarantees every $k \in [i_t + 1, p - 1]$ has $\text{rk}[k] > \text{rk}[i_t]$ while $\text{rk}[p] < \text{rk}[i_t]$!
3. Once $\text{SA}[1..N]$ and $\text{rk}[1..N]$ are fixed, greedily assign $S[\text{SA}[1]] = 1$ and for $t = 2 \dots N$:
   $$S[\text{SA}[t]] = S[\text{SA}[t-1]] + \bigl[\text{rk}[\text{SA}[t-1] + 1] > \text{rk}[\text{SA}[t] + 1]\bigr],$$
   which is the standard $O(N)$ minimal-alphabet Suffix Array realization!
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-II-04"}
#### 1. Target Paradigm & Diagnostic Breakdown

- **Source / Origin**: Universal Cup / QOJ — *Inverse Strict-Minimal-Suffix Span Reconstruction* (`W1B-10`).
- **Target Chapter**: `Ch 07` (`Theorem 7.1` Next-Smaller-Suffix Identity $\text{nsv}[i] = i + \lambda[i]$ & Min-Cartesian Tree / Suffix Array Reconstruction).
- **Key Insight**: Because suffixes of $S[1..N]$ are all distinct in length, two suffixes $S[i..N]$ and $S[j..N]$ ($i \ne j$) can **never be equal**! Therefore, $\text{nsv}[i] = i + \ell_i$ means $\text{rk}[j] > \text{rk}[i]$ for all $j \in [i+1, i+\ell_i-1]$ and $\text{rk}[i+\ell_i] < \text{rk}[i]$ (with $\text{rk}[N+1] = 0$).

#### 2. Complete Proof of Laminar Necessity & Sufficiency

1. **Laminar Check**:
   Maintain a decreasing stack of active right boundaries $p_s$. For $i = 1 \dots N$:

   - Pop all $p_s = i$ from the stack.
   - Let $p = i + \ell_i$. If $p > \text{top}(\text{stack})$, the interval $[i, p-1]$ properly crosses the enclosing interval ending at $\text{top}(\text{stack}) - 1$, which is impossible; return `-1`.
   - Push $p$ onto the stack and add $i$ to the child list of $p$.
2. **Unique Suffix Rank Permutation $\text{SA}[1..N]$ from the $\text{nsv}$ Tree**:
   For each vertex $u \in \{1, \dots, N+1\}$, its children $c_1 < c_2 < \cdots < c_d$ partition the interval $[u_{\text{left}}, u - 1]$ into contiguous subtrees $\text{Sub}(c_t) = [c_t, c_{t+1} - 1]$ (where $c_{d+1} = u$).

   - Within $\text{Sub}(c_t) = [c_t, c_{t+1} - 1]$, $c_t$ must have the **minimum** rank so that $\text{rk}[j] > \text{rk}[c_t]$ for all $j \in [c_t + 1, c_{t+1} - 1]$.
   - Across siblings $c_1 < c_2 < \cdots < c_d$, to ensure that for every $x \in \text{Sub}(c_a)$ its first smaller suffix to the right lies inside $\text{Sub}(c_a) \cup \{u\}$ (and never inside $\text{Sub}(c_b)$ for $a < b$), we must assign **all ranks in $\text{Sub}(c_a)$ to be strictly smaller than all ranks in $\text{Sub}(c_b)$** for $a < b$?
   - **Sibling Ordering Verification**: For $c_a < c_b$, $c_b$ lies inside $[c_a + 1, u - 1]$! Since $\text{nsv}[c_a] = u$, we require $\text{rk}[j] > \text{rk}[c_a]$ for **all** $j \in [c_a + 1, u - 1]$, which includes $\text{Sub}(c_b)$ ($b > a$)!
   - Could a node $x \in \text{Sub}(c_a)$ have $\text{nsv}[x] = c_{a+1}$? In the laminar check, every interval $[x, \text{nsv}[x] - 1]$ for $x \in [c_a, c_{a+1} - 1]$ has $\text{nsv}[x] \le c_{a+1}$—in fact, since $c_{a+1} > c_a$ has $\text{nsv}[c_a] = u > c_{a+1}$, no $x \in [c_a, c_{a+1}-1]$ can have $\text{nsv}[x] = c_{a+1}$ (for $x > c_a$, laminarity inside $[c_a, u-1]$ guarantees that $\text{nsv}[x]$ is an ancestor of $x$ inside $[c_a+1, u]$, so $\text{nsv}[x]$ can only equal $u$ if $x$ is one of the direct children $c_b$ of $u$!).
   - Therefore, for every $x \in \text{Sub}(c_a) = [c_a, c_{a+1} - 1]$ with $x > c_a$, its parent $\text{nsv}[x]$ lies **strictly inside $[c_a + 1, c_{a+1} - 1]$** (never equal to $c_{a+1}$)!
   - Hence, ordering every node $u$ first, followed by $\text{Sub}(c_1), \text{Sub}(c_2), \dots, \text{Sub}(c_d)$ in **increasing order of child index $c_1 < c_2 < \cdots < c_d$**, satisfies:
     1. $\text{rk}[u] < \text{rk}[y]$ for all $y \in \text{Sub}(u) \setminus \{u\}$, and
     2. $\text{rk}[\text{Sub}(c_1)] < \text{rk}[\text{Sub}(c_2)] < \cdots < \text{rk}[\text{Sub}(c_d)]$, so for every $x \in \text{Sub}(c_a)$, all indices $y \in [c_{a+1}, u - 1]$ have $\text{rk}[y] > \text{rk}[x]$, meaning the first index $> x$ with rank $< \text{rk}[x]$ is identical to its first smaller index inside $\text{Sub}(c_a) \cup \{u\}$, which is $\text{nsv}[x]$!
3. **Minimal Alphabet Realization from $\text{SA}[1..N]$**:
   Set $\text{rk}[N+1] = 0$. Set $S[\text{SA}[1]] = 1$. For $t = 2 \dots N$, two adjacent suffixes $\text{SA}[t-1]$ and $\text{SA}[t]$ in sorted order can share the same first character $S[\text{SA}[t]] = S[\text{SA}[t-1]]$ if and only if their stripped suffixes satisfy $\text{rk}[\text{SA}[t-1] + 1] < \text{rk}[\text{SA}[t] + 1]$; otherwise we must increment the character by $+1$.
    This both minimizes $\sigma = S[\text{SA}[N]]$ and produces the componentwise lexicographically smallest string $S[1..N]$ in $O(N)$ time!
::::

### Problem `CP-II-05` — Minimum-Diversity Duplicate-Piece Substring Partition

> **Statement**: You are given a string $S[1..N]$ ($1 \le N \le 2 \times 10^5$) over an alphabet of size $|\Sigma| \le 26$ and $Q$ online queries ($1 \le Q \le 2 \times 10^5$). Each query specifies a substring $U = S[l..r]$ ($1 \le l \le r \le N$).
>
> You must partition $U$ into $k \ge 2$ non-empty contiguous pieces $U = P_1 P_2 \cdots P_k$ such that **at least two pieces are identical strings** ($P_a = P_b$ for some $1 \le a < b \le k$). Over all valid partitions of $U$, find the **minimum possible number of distinct strings** in the multiset $\{P_1, P_2, \dots, P_k\}$ (or output `-1` if no valid partition exists).
>
> **Constraints**: $1 \le N, Q \le 2 \times 10^5$, $|\Sigma| \le 26$, time limit $3.0\text{ s}$, memory limit $256\text{ MB}$.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}
- **Decoy Elimination**: This is *not* a global dynamic programming problem over $[l, r]$; because $|\Sigma| \le 26$, the answer is bounded by a small constant and reduces to testing periodic powers, squares, and borders inside $U = S[l..r]$ (`Ch 08` + `Ch 01`).
- **Diagnostic Signal**: When does a valid partition exist at all?
  - If all characters in $U = S[l..r]$ are distinct (only possible when $|U| \le 26$), no two disjoint non-empty pieces can ever share even their first character, so the answer is `-1`.
  - Otherwise, some character $c$ appears at least twice in $U$, say at positions $x < y$. Splitting $U$ around single-character pieces $S[x]$ and $S[y]$ gives at most $5$ pieces $U[1..x-1] \mid c \mid U[x+1..y-1] \mid c \mid U[y+1..|U|]$, which contains at most **4 distinct strings**! Thus the answer is always in $\{-1, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$.
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}
**Exact Characterization of $d \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$**: Classify the minimum number of distinct strings $d \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ for $U = S[l..r]$:

- **$d = 1$**: $U = A^k$ for some $k \ge 2$ (tested by checking prime divisors $p \mid |U|$ via $O(1)$ LCE: $\text{LCP}(l, l + |U|/p) \ge |U| - |U|/p$).
- **$d = 2$**: $U$ has the form $A^k B$ (**starts with a square $AA$**), $B A^k$ (**ends with a square $AA$**), or $A B A$ (**has a nonempty proper border $A$**; if the border overlaps itself, $U$ begins with a square anyway!).
- **$d = 3$**: Either $S[l]$ appears again in $S[l+1..r]$, or $S[r]$ appears again in $S[l..r-1]$, or $U = B A A C$ (**$U$ contains a square $AA$ somewhere strictly inside $[l, r]$**).
- **$d = 4$**: None of the above hold, and $|U|$ has at least one repeated character.
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}
How do we test in $O(1)$ per query whether $S[l..r]$ starts with a square, ends with a square, or contains a square?

1. Enumerate all **Runs** $R = [l_R, r_R, p] \in \mathcal{R}(S)$ in $O(N)$ time (`Ch 08`).
2. Every minimal square starting at $x$ or ending at $y$ is primitively rooted inside some run $R = [l_R, r_R, p]$. Sort all runs by increasing $2p$ and use two **DSU skip-lists** to assign `min_sq_start[x] = 2p` for $x \in [l_R, r_R - 2p + 1]$ and `min_sq_end[y] = 2p` for $y \in [l_R + 2p - 1, r_R]$ in $O(N \alpha(N))$ total time!
3. Then:
   - $S[l..r]$ starts with a square $\iff l + \text{min\_sq\_start}[l] - 1 \le r$.
   - $S[l..r]$ ends with a square $\iff r - \text{min\_sq\_end}[r] + 1 \ge l$.
   - $S[l..r]$ contains a square $\iff \min_{x \in [l, r]} \bigl(x + \text{min\_sq\_start}[x] - 1\bigr) \le r$ (a single $O(1)$ RMQ query!).
   - Finally, test whether $S[l..r]$ has a nonempty border (`ABA`) in $O(\sqrt{N})$ time via BSGS (check border lengths $\le \sqrt{N}$ directly, and check SA ranks within $\pm \sqrt{N}$ of $\text{rk}[l]$) or $O(\log N)$ via IPM!
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-II-05"}
#### 1. Target Paradigm & Diagnostic Breakdown

- **Source / Origin**: Codeforces 1043G — *Speckled Band* (`W1B-14`).
- **Target Chapters**: `Ch 08` (Runs Enumeration & DSU Skip-List Square Covering) + `Ch 01`/`Ch 02` (Substring Periodicity & Border Testing).
- **Why Naive Square Marking Fails**: A single string can have $\Theta(N^2)$ square occurrences; however, by **Corollary 8.2(1) (`Ch 08`)**, the sum of primitively rooted square start intervals across all runs satisfies $\sum_{R \in \mathcal{R}(S)} (r_R - l_R - 2p + 2) < 2N$! That means even a plain loop over $x \in [l_R, r_R - 2p + 1]$ across all runs takes **strictly less than $2N$ iterations in total** without even needing a DSU! (Though a DSU skip-list is also $O(N)$ and immediately gives the minimum $2p$).

#### 2. Complete Decision Waterfall for Query $[l, r]$ ($L = r - l + 1$)

1. **Check $d = -1$**: Using $26$ prefix-sum arrays `cnt[c][1..N]`, if every character $c \in [0, 25]$ has $\text{cnt}[c][r] - \text{cnt}[c][l-1] \le 1$, return `-1`.
2. **Check $d = 1$ ($S[l..r] = A^k, k \ge 2$)**: Precompute smallest prime factors `spf[1..N]`. For each distinct prime divisor $q \mid L$, if $\text{LCP}(l, l + L/q) \ge L - L/q$, return `1`.
3. **Check $d = 2$ ($A^k B$, $B A^k$, or $A B A$)**:
   - Notice any $A^k B$ ($k \ge 2$) is also a 2-distinct-piece partition $A \mid A \mid B$ (if $k=2$) or $A \mid \cdots \mid A \mid B$, which holds iff $S[l..r]$ **starts with a square** ($l + \text{min\_sq\_start}[l] - 1 \le r$).
   - Symmetrically, $B A^k$ holds iff $S[l..r]$ **ends with a square** ($r - \text{min\_sq\_end}[r] + 1 \ge l$).
   - For $A B A$ with $|A| < L/2$: test if $S[l..r]$ has a border of length $b \in [1, \lfloor (L-1)/2 \rfloor]$:
     - For $b \le B_{\text{thresh}} = \sqrt{N}$: test $\text{LCP}(l, r - b + 1) \ge b$ in $O(1)$.
     - For $b > B_{\text{thresh}}$: any such border $j = r - b + 1 \in [l + 1, r - B_{\text{thresh}}]$ satisfies $\text{LCP}(l, j) \ge b > B_{\text{thresh}}$. Since at most $N / B_{\text{thresh}} = \sqrt{N}$ disjoint suffixes can jump by $B_{\text{thresh}}$, scan the Suffix Array outward from $\text{rk}[l]$ while $\text{LCP}(l, \text{SA}[t]) > B_{\text{thresh}}$ (or check at most $2\sqrt{N}$ neighbors in SA; if more than $2\sqrt{N}$ neighbors have $\text{LCP} > \sqrt{N}$, they form a periodic run already caught by the square check!).
   - If any of the three holds, return `2`.
4. **Check $d = 3$ ($c B c$, $B c c$, $c c B$, or $B A A C$)**:
   - Check if $\text{cnt}[S[l]][r] - \text{cnt}[S[l]][l] \ge 1$ (first character repeats) or $\text{cnt}[S[r]][r-1] - \text{cnt}[S[r]][l-1] \ge 1$ (last character repeats).
   - Check if $S[l..r]$ contains any square via a single RMQ query: $\min_{x \in [l, r]} (x + \text{min\_sq\_start}[x] - 1) \le r$.
   - If any holds, return `3`.
5. **Otherwise**: Return `4`.

#### 3. Complexity Audit

- **Preprocessing**: $O(N \log N)$ for SA + RMQ and Runs Enumeration; $O(N)$ to populate `min_sq_start` and `min_sq_end` (by Corollary 8.2(3), $\sum_{R \in \mathcal{R}(S)} (r_R - l_R - 2p + 2) < 2N$).
- **Query Time**: $O(|\Sigma| + \sqrt{N})$ (or $O(|\Sigma| + \log N)$ with IPM), easily passing within $3.0\text{ s}$.
::::

### Problem `CP-II-06` — Tandem-Free Substring Range Counting

> **Statement**: A string $W$ is called **tandem-free (square-free)** if it contains no contiguous substring of the form $u u$ for any non-empty string $u \in \Sigma^+$.
>
> You are given a string $S[1..N]$ ($1 \le N \le 5 \times 10^5$) and $Q$ queries ($1 \le Q \le 5 \times 10^5$). Each query provides a range $[L_q, R_q]$ ($1 \le L_q \le R_q \le N$) and asks for the number of index pairs $(a, b)$ satisfying $L_q \le a \le b \le R_q$ such that the substring $S[a..b]$ is tandem-free.
>
> **Constraints**: $1 \le N, Q \le 5 \times 10^5$, time limit $2.0\text{ s}$, memory limit $256\text{ MB}$.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}
- **Decoy Elimination**: Unlike `CP-II-07` (which counts distinct square strings $w^2$ inside $[L_q, R_q]$), this problem counts **sub-intervals $[a, b] \subseteq [L_q, R_q]$** that avoid all squares $u u$. Because square-freeness is hereditary under taking substrings, we do not need a 2D Fenwick sweep!
- **Diagnostic Signal**: If $S[a..b]$ contains a square $u u$, then so does $S[a..b']$ for every $b' \ge b$, and so does $S[a'..b]$ for every $a' \le a$. For each left endpoint $a \in [1, N]$, let $F[a]$ be the **smallest right endpoint $b \ge a$** such that $S[a..b]$ contains a square (or $F[a] = N + 1$ if $S[a..N]$ is square-free):
  1. Why is $F[1] \le F[2] \le \cdots \le F[N]$ monotonically non-decreasing?
  2. How does every minimal square inside $S$ relate to the set of Runs $\mathcal{R}(S)$ (`Ch 08`)?
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}
**Primitively Rooted Squares & Linear Horizon Bound**: Every non-primitive square $(w^k)^2 = w^{2k}$ ($k \ge 2$) already contains the shorter primitive square $w^2$ at its very start! Therefore, $S[a..b]$ is square-free if and only if it contains no **primitively rooted** square $S[x..x+2p-1]$ ($a \le x$ and $x + 2p - 1 \le b$).
For each index $x \in [1, N]$, let $M[x]$ be the minimum right endpoint $x + 2p - 1$ of a primitive square starting at $x$ (so $F[a] = \min_{x \ge a} M[x]$).
Each run $R = [l_R, r_R, p] \in \mathcal{R}(S)$ contributes the update:
$$M[x] \gets \min\bigl(M[x],\; x + 2p - 1\bigr) \qquad \forall x \in [l_R,\; r_R - 2p + 1].$$
By **Corollary 8.2(3) (`Ch 08`)**, $\sum_{R \in \mathcal{R}(S)} (r_R - l_R - 2p + 2) < 2N$, so you can loop over $x \in [l_R, r_R - 2p + 1]$ directly in $< 2N$ total steps!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}

1. Enumerate all runs $R = [l_R, r_R, p] \in \mathcal{R}(S)$ in $O(N)$ time (`Ch 08` Method B).
2. Initialize $M[x] = N + 1$. For each run $R = [l_R, r_R, p]$ and each $x \in [l_R, r_R - 2p + 1]$ (total loop iterations $< 2N$ by Corollary 8.2(3)!), set $M[x] \gets \min(M[x], x + 2p - 1)$.
3. Compute the suffix minimums $F[a] = \min(M[a], F[a+1])$ for $a = N$ down to $1$.
4. For a query $[L_q, R_q]$, $S[a..b]$ ($L_q \le a \le b \le R_q$) is tandem-free $\iff b \le \min(R_q, F[a] - 1)$. Since $F[a]$ is non-decreasing, binary search for the unique split point $m^* \in [L_q - 1, R_q]$ where $F[a] - 1 \le R_q$:
   $$\text{Ans}(L_q, R_q) = \sum_{a = L_q}^{m^*} \bigl(F[a] - a\bigr) + \sum_{a = m^* + 1}^{R_q} \bigl(R_q - a + 1\bigr),$$
   evaluated in $O(\log N)$ (or $O(1)$ using an inverse lookup table `first_ge[R_q]`!) using prefix sums of $F[a] - a$.
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-II-06"}
#### 1. Target Paradigm & Diagnostic Breakdown

- **Source / Origin**: Universal Cup / QOJ — *Square-Free Substring Range Queries* (`W1B-18`).
- **Target Chapter**: `Ch 08` (Bannai et al. Runs Theorem `Theorem 8.1` & The $< 2N$ Primitively Rooted Square Starts Bound `Corollary 8.2(3)`).
- **Contrast with `Ch 08` Ladder (`W1B-19`)**: While `W1B-19` uses the left-horizon $L_{\max}[r]$ to count global square-free partitions of $S[1..N]$ via 1D DP, range substring queries $[L_q, R_q]$ decouple into independent intervals $[a, \min(R_q, F[a] - 1)]$ for each $a \in [L_q, R_q]$.

#### 2. Mathematical Proof of $O(N)$ Horizon Construction & $O(1)$ Query Evaluation

1. **Primitivity Reduction**: Suppose $S[a..b]$ contains a square $S[x..x+2d-1] = u^2$. Let $w$ be the primitive root of $u$ ($u = w^k, |w| = p, d = kp$). Then $S[x..x+2p-1] = w^2$ is a primitively rooted square contained inside $S[x..x+2d-1] \subseteq S[a..b]$ with $x + 2p - 1 \le x + 2d - 1 \le b$. Thus minimal square right-endpoints are determined exclusively by primitively rooted squares ($k = 1$).
2. **Linear Total Work Across Runs**: Every primitively rooted square $S[x..x+2p-1]$ is a sub-interval of a unique run $R = [l_R, r_R, p] \in \mathcal{R}(S)$ with $x \in [l_R, r_R - 2p + 1]$. By **Corollary 8.2(3)** of `Ch 08`,
   $$\sum_{R = [l_R, r_R, p] \in \mathcal{R}(S)} (r_R - l_R - 2p + 2) \le 2(N - 1) < 2N.$$
   Thus a direct nested loop over $R \in \mathcal{R}(S)$ and $x \in [l_R, r_R - 2p + 1]$ setting $M[x] = \min(M[x], x + 2p - 1)$ executes **fewer than $2N$ inner-loop steps** across the entire algorithm!

3. **$O(1)$ Query via Monotone Split Lookup**:
   Since $F[a] = \min_{x \ge a} M[x]$ satisfies $a + 1 \le F[a] \le N + 1$ and $F[1] \le F[2] \le \cdots \le F[N]$, we can precompute for each $R \in [1, N]$ the largest index $\text{split}[R] = \max\{a \in [1, N] \mid F[a] - 1 \le R\}$ in $O(N)$ time via a two-pointer scan.
   For any query $[L_q, R_q]$, clamp $m^* = \text{clamp}(\text{split}[R_q], L_q - 1, R_q)$ and return:
   $$\bigl(\text{pref}_F[m^*] - \text{pref}_F[L_q - 1]\bigr) + \frac{(R_q - m^*)(R_q - m^* + 1)}{2},$$
   where $\text{pref}_F[k] = \sum_{a=1}^k (F[a] - a)$.

#### 3. Complexity & Pitfall Audit

- **Time Complexity**: $O(N)$ preprocessing (with $O(N)$ SA + Lyndon-array Runs enumeration) and **$O(1)$ time per query** ($O(N + Q)$ total time!).
- **Pitfall Guard**: Remember that the smallest possible square has length $2$ ($p = 1$), so $F[a] \ge a + 1$ always holds (every single character $S[a..a]$ of length $1$ is tandem-free).
::::

### Problem `CP-II-07` — Range Distinct Tandem Repeats & Clipped Periodic Exponent Sum

> **Statement**: You are given a string $S[1..N]$ ($1 \le N \le 2 \times 10^5$) and $Q$ queries ($1 \le Q \le 2 \times 10^5$). Each query specifies a substring $U = S[L_q..R_q]$ ($1 \le L_q \le R_q \le N$) and asks you to compute two structural invariants of $U$:
>
> 1. **$D(L_q, R_q)$**: The number of **distinct strings** $X$ of the form $X = w w$ ($w \in \Sigma^+$) that occur at least once as a contiguous substring of $S[L_q..R_q]$.
> 2. **$E(L_q, R_q)$**: Let $\mathcal{R}(U)$ be the set of all maximal periodic substrings of $U = S[L_q..R_q]$ (each defined by a sub-interval $[l, r] \subseteq [L_q, R_q]$ and its shortest period $p$ such that $r - l + 1 \ge 2p$ and the period $p$ cannot be extended left inside $[L_q, l-1]$ or right inside $[r+1, R_q]$). Compute
>    $$E(L_q, R_q) = \sum_{[l, r, p] \in \mathcal{R}(S[L_q..R_q])} \left\lfloor \frac{r - l + 1 - p}{p} \right\rfloor.$$
>
> **Constraints**: $1 \le N, Q \le 2 \times 10^5$, time limit $3.0\text{ s}$, memory limit $512\text{ MB}$.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}
- **Decoy Elimination (Decoy Pair II)**: In Part 1 ($D(L_q, R_q)$), why can't we simply sum over runs? Because the **same square $w^2$** can repeat at $a, a+p, a+2p, \dots$ inside a single run AND can also appear in completely separate runs elsewhere in $S$!
- **Diagnostic Signal**: Look at the two quantities requested for $U = S[L_q..R_q]$:
  1. In Part 2 ($E(L_q, R_q)$), for any run $R' = [l, r, p] \in \mathcal{R}(U)$, $\lfloor (r - l + 1 - p)/p \rfloor = \lfloor \text{exp}(R') - 1 \rfloor$ counts the number of harmonic multiples $kp \le r - l + 1$ ($k \ge 2$) inside the clipped run!
  2. In Part 1 ($D(L_q, R_q)$), how many canonical square representatives exist across all runs (`Ch 08`), and how do intra-run periodic shifts $y - p \to y$ behave in the $(L, R)$-plane?
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}
**The $< 2N$ Representative Squares & Shift-by-$p$ Progression**: For Part 1 ($D(L_q, R_q)$), sweep the query right endpoint $r = 1 \to N$, maintaining $+1$ in a Fenwick tree at the **latest starting position** `last_start(w^2)` of each distinct square $w^2$ ending at or before $r$:

1. By the **$< 2N$ Representative Squares Lemma (`Ch 08`, `Corollary 8.2(3)` / `§2.4`)**, across all runs $R = [l_R, r_R, p]$ and all harmonics $d = kp \le (r_R - l_R + 1)/2$, there are strictly fewer than $2N$ canonical phase representatives $a \in [l_R, \min(l_R + p - 1, r_R - 2d + 1)]$.
2. What about the remaining square occurrences $y \in [l_R + p, r_R - 2d + 1]$ inside the same run $(R, d)$? Every such occurrence $S[y..y+2d-1]$ has an **identical previous occurrence at $y - p \ge l_R$ inside the exact same run $R$**!
3. Therefore:
   - Only the $< 2N$ canonical representatives $a \in [l_R, \min(l_R + p - 1, r_R - 2d + 1)]$ ever need a global lookup (via SAM node or 64-bit double rolling hash / SA equivalence class) to find their previous occurrence in an *earlier* run!
   - Every non-canonical shift $y \in [l_R + p, r_R - 2d + 1]$ simply moves its $+1$ marker from $y - p$ to $y$ when $r$ reaches $y + 2d - 1$, which is a contiguous diagonal segment as $r$ sweeps from $l_R + p + 2d - 1$ to $r_R$!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}

1. **Compiling Part 1 ($D(L_q, R_q)$)**:
   - As $r$ sweeps across $[l_R + 2d - 1, r_R]$, inserting $+1$ at $x = r - 2d + 1$ for $r \in [l_R + 2d - 1, r_R]$ and inserting $-1$ at $x' = r - 2d + 1 - p$ for $r \in [l_R + p + 2d - 1, r_R]$ are **two slope-1 diagonal segment updates**, while the $< 2N$ cross-run deduplications (removing the last occurrence $x_{\text{prev}}$ of the previous run when $a + 2d - 1$ is reached) are $< 2N$ point updates!
2. **Compiling Part 2 ($E(L_q, R_q)$)**:
   - By the **Fine–Wilf Clipping Non-Collision Lemma (`Ch 08`)**, the runs of $S[L_q..R_q]$ are in 1-to-1 correspondence with global runs $R = [l_R, r_R, p] \in \mathcal{R}(S)$ whose clipped interval $[l', r'] = [\max(L_q, l_R), \min(R_q, r_R)]$ has length $M = r' - l' + 1 \ge 2p$.
   - Since $\lfloor \frac{M - p}{p} \rfloor \cdot [M \ge 2p] = \sum_{k=2}^{\lfloor M/p \rfloor} 1 = \#\{k \ge 2 \mid M \ge kp\}$, exchanging the sum over $R \in \mathcal{R}(S)$ and harmonics $k = 2, \dots, \lfloor \text{exp}(R) \rfloor$ yields:
     $$E(L_q, R_q) = \sum_{R = [l_R, r_R, p] \in \mathcal{R}(S)} \;\sum_{k = 2}^{\lfloor (r_R - l_R + 1)/p \rfloor} \bigl[\min(R_q, r_R) - \max(L_q, l_R) + 1 \ge kp\bigr],$$
     which has **at most $\sum_{R \in \mathcal{R}(S)} (\lfloor \text{exp}(R) \rfloor - 1) \le N - 1$ pairs $(R, k)$ in total** by Corollary 8.2(2)!
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-II-07"}
#### 1. Target Paradigm & Diagnostic Breakdown

- **Source / Origin**: Synthesis of `[国家集训队论文 2019 — 金策]` LOJ 6681 (`W1B-23`) & Interior Root Range Sum (`W1B-42`).
- **Target Chapters**: `Ch 08` (The Runs Theorem `Theorem 8.1` / `Corollary 8.2`, Fine–Wilf Clipping Non-Collision, and $< 2N$ Representative Squares) + `Ch 07` (Double-Order Lyndon Array Seeding).
- **Two Miraculous Linear-Bound Reductions**:
  1. For $E(L_q, R_q)$, using the identity $\lfloor \frac{M - p}{p} \rfloor \cdot [M \ge 2p] = \sum_{k \ge 2} [M \ge kp]$ decomposes $E(L_q, R_q)$ into at most $\sum_{R} (\lfloor \text{exp}(R) \rfloor - 1) \le N - 1$ 3-sided dominance rectangles $(R, k)$!
  2. For $D(L_q, R_q)$, separating intra-run periodic shifts $y - p \to y$ from the $< 2N$ inter-run canonical representatives $(R, d = mp, a)$ reduces range distinct squares to $< 1.5N$ diagonal segment updates plus $< 2N$ point updates!

#### 2. Complete Compilation of Part 2: $E(L_q, R_q)$ via $\le N - 1$ Harmonic Rectangles
By the Fine–Wilf Clipping Non-Collision Lemma, no two distinct global runs $R_1, R_2 \in \mathcal{R}(S)$ ($p_1 < p_2$) can clip to the same sub-interval of length $\ge 2p_2$ inside $[L_q, R_q]$. For each global run $R = [l_R, r_R, p]$, let $M_R(L_q, R_q) = \min(R_q, r_R) - \max(L_q, l_R) + 1$. Then:
$$E(L_q, R_q) = \sum_{R = [l_R, r_R, p] \in \mathcal{R}(S)} \;\sum_{k = 2}^{\lfloor (r_R - l_R + 1)/p \rfloor} \bigl[M_R(L_q, R_q) \ge kp\bigr].$$
For a fixed pair $(R, k)$ ($2 \le k \le \lfloor (r_R - l_R + 1)/p \rfloor$, total pairs $\le N - 1$), let $W = kp$. The condition $\min(R_q, r_R) - \max(L_q, l_R) + 1 \ge W$ holds if and only if:
$$L_q \le r_R - W + 1, \qquad R_q \ge l_R + W - 1, \qquad \text{and} \qquad R_q - L_q + 1 \ge W.$$
Notice that $L_q \le r_R - W + 1$ and $R_q \ge l_R + W - 1$ automatically imply $R_q - L_q + 1 \ge W$ **unless** $l_R < L_q \le R_q < r_R$ with $R_q - L_q + 1 < W$. Thus:
$$\bigl[M_R(L_q, R_q) \ge W\bigr] = \bigl[L_q \le r_R - W + 1 \;\wedge\; R_q \ge l_R + W - 1\bigr] - \bigl[L_q > l_R \;\wedge\; R_q < r_R \;\wedge\; R_q - L_q + 1 < W\bigr].$$

- The first term is a standard 2D dominance count over $\le N - 1$ points $(r_R - W + 1,\; l_R + W - 1)$, answered offline in $O((N + Q) \log N)$ via a Fenwick tree sweeping $R_q = 1 \to N$.
- The second term is a 2D containment query filtered by $W > R_q - L_q + 1$: notice that whenever the first condition $L_q \le r_R - W + 1$ and $R_q \ge l_R + W - 1$ holds together with $R_q - L_q + 1 < W$, we automatically have:
  $$L_q > R_q - W + 1 \ge (l_R + W - 1) - W + 1 = l_R, \qquad R_q < L_q + W - 1 \le (r_R - W + 1) + W - 1 = r_R!$$
  Inside any run $R = [l_R, r_R, p]$ that strictly contains $[L_q, R_q]$ ($l_R < L_q \le R_q < r_R$), the clipped interval is simply $[L_q, R_q]$ itself, so its true contribution to $E(L_q, R_q)$ is $\max(0, \lfloor (R_q - L_q + 1 - p)/p \rfloor)$, whereas the first term counts all $W = kp$ ($k \ge 2$) satisfying $L_q \le r_R - W + 1$ and $R_q \ge l_R + W - 1$. Subtracting the overcounted pairs via an offline sweep by $W > R_q - L_q + 1$ (or handling the containing run $l_R < L_q \le R_q < r_R$ separately) runs in $O((N + Q) \log N)$ time.

#### 3. Complete Compilation of Part 1: $D(L_q, R_q)$ in $O((N + Q) \log N)$

1. Enumerate all runs $R = [l_R, r_R, p]$ in $O(N)$ time, sorted by left endpoint $l_R$.
2. For each run $R$ and each harmonic $d = mp \le (r_R - l_R + 1)/2$:
   - Add a positive slope-1 diagonal segment $[(l_R, l_R + 2d - 1) \to (r_R - 2d + 1, r_R)]$ with weight $+1$.
   - If $r_R - l_R + 1 \ge 2d + p$, add a negative slope-1 diagonal segment $[(l_R, l_R + p + 2d - 1) \to (r_R - 2d + 1 - p, r_R)]$ with weight $-1$ (which cancels the previous occurrence $y - p$ inside $R$ as soon as the shift $y$ finishes at $r = y + 2d - 1$).
   - For each canonical phase representative $a \in [l_R, \min(l_R + p - 1, r_R - 2d + 1)]$ (total $< 2N$ across the whole string):
     - Identify the substring $S[a..a+2d-1]$ by its SAM state + length $(u, 2d)$ (found via offline tree-walk or binary lifting on the SAM Link Tree).
     - Look up the previous run's rightmost occurrence start `last_occ[(u, 2d)]`. If `last_occ` exists at $x_{\text{prev}}$, emit a point update of weight $-1$ at $(x = x_{\text{prev}}, r = a + 2d - 1)$ (cancelling the previous run's last copy when the new run's first copy completes at $a + 2d - 1$).
     - Update `last_occ[(u, 2d)]` to the last occurrence of this phase inside $R$: $a + \lfloor (r_R - 2d + 1 - a)/p \rfloor \cdot p$.
3. Sweep $r = 1 \to N$ maintaining two Fenwick trees (encoding linear coefficients $A \cdot L_q + B$ for active diagonal segments and completed point updates), answering all $Q$ queries $D(L_q, R_q)$ in $O((N + Q) \log N)$ time and $O(N)$ space!
